headline: Cloudflare acquires Deno, shutting down Deno Deploy in 6 months; entire team joins
summary: Cloudflare has acquired Deno, integrating its team and celld technology into the Workers platform. Deno Deploy will shut down by April 2027, and the Deno runtime will cease development by October 2027.
details: Cloudflare announced on October 9 its acquisition of Deno, bringing the entire Deno team, including Node.js creator Ryan Dahl, into Cloudflare. This move has significant implications for developers using Deno for edge deployments.

Deno Deploy is scheduled to shut down in six months, around April 2027. The Deno runtime will receive monthly patches for one more year, until approximately October 2027, after which its development will end.

Cloudflare's primary interest in Deno was its team and `celld`, an open-source technology for self-hosting the Workers programming model. JSR, Deno's package registry, is expected to survive the acquisition.

`celld`, released by Deno in August 2026, offers an open-source implementation of the Workers and Durable Objects programming model that can run on user-owned infrastructure. This addresses a key limitation in Cloudflare's `workerd` runtime for scalable, self-hosted Durable Objects.

The strategic plan is to merge `celld`'s innovations and code into `workerd`, making self-hosting Workers and Durable Objects a fully supported option. Ryan Dahl stated the team's goal is to make the Workers programming model a mainstream way to build servers.

This acquisition reshapes the long-standing criticism of Workers' vendor lock-in. While the APIs remain Cloudflare-specific, the integration of `celld` into `workerd` provides a credible path to running the full Workers model off Cloudflare's network.

Developers are advised to adopt portable coding practices, such as using web-standard fetch handlers and isolating platform bindings behind small interfaces. This approach ensures flexibility and a dramatically cheaper exit strategy if future platform changes necessitate it.

headline_marked: [[Built a private, local AI bookkeeper]] and learned where small models truly excel
headline: Built a private, local AI bookkeeper and learned where small models truly excel
summary: A developer built an offline, local-first AI bookkeeper to categorize transactions and answer financial questions without data leaving the laptop. Benchmarking revealed the true strength of small language models.
details: Freelancers often struggle with tax-time transaction categorization. This project, "Deductible," offers a local-first AI bookkeeping copilot to simplify this process. It categorizes transactions and generates Schedule-C-ready CSVs.
Deductible runs entirely offline on an open-weight LLM (Qwen2.5 via llama-cpp-python, GGUF), ensuring no network access, API keys, or per-row costs. All financial data remains on the user's machine.

Initial benchmarking showed that small models struggled with direct transaction classification. The developer realized the model's true value lies in natural language interaction, explaining and advising on precomputed financial snapshots.

The architecture now splits tasks: auditable Python handles all calculations and deterministic classification, while the LLM focuses on language-based queries. This ensures reliability for sensitive financial data.

The project was built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge. The next step involves real-world testing with a freelancer to gather feedback and explore fine-tuning paths for recurring vendors.
